summary:
Rivers State lies inside Nigeria and takes its governing law from national instruments rather than any local statute. The Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, signed by President Goodluck Jonathan in January 2014, applies there, as does the Nigerian Criminal Code in the form used across the country's southern states. The sources assembled here record no Rivers-specific provision, incident series or enforcement divergence, so a visitor to Port Harcourt should expect the national rules to govern.

The 2014 Act reaches well past marriage. It makes same-sex marriage and civil unions invalid and illegal, and it criminalises registering, operating, participating in or supporting gay clubs, societies or organisations. Human Rights Watch's October 2016 report sets 10 to 14 years' imprisonment for those organisational offences and records that the Act also bans same-sex cohabitation and any public show of a same-sex amorous relationship. UK Foreign, Commonwealth and Development Office travel advice, updated in August 2026, adds that the Act extends to helpers and attendees of same-sex weddings.

In the south, where Rivers sits, the Criminal Code criminalises sex between men with penalties of up to 14 years' imprisonment and treats gross indecency as an offence carrying up to 3 years. Sharia criminalisation in twelve northern Nigerian states reaches same-sex acts between men and between women, with male sodomy punishable by death under state Zina provisions. That northern exposure is not the law in Rivers, but it shapes onward travel inside the country.

One provisional narrowing exists. In 2022 a group of Nigerian human rights organisations and activists sued over Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act, and the court ruled those sections unconstitutional and unenforceable nationwide, removing them as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals. The ruling does not decriminalise same-sex conduct; the marriage, civil union and cohabitation bans and the wider criminal code remain.

Nigeria offers no legal protections for LGBTQ+ people of any kind, and police practice after the 2014 Act has been documented. Human Rights Watch records arbitrary arrest and extortion as commonplace, including eight of the 21 young men arrested but never charged at a birthday party in Ibadan. The same report documents an attack inside Rivers State itself: Daniel, a 21-year-old gay man from Lagos, travelled to Port Harcourt in January 2015 to meet someone he had contacted on Facebook, and was attacked and sexually abused there. He did not report the assault to the police.

The UK travel advisory of August 2026 warns LGBT+ travellers to Nigeria of arrest, violence, attacks, blackmail and intimidation, of up to 14 years' imprisonment for same-sex activity, and of death-penalty exposure under Sharia law in northern states. A trans or gender-nonconforming visitor to Port Harcourt faces the same criminal framework plus the documented risk of violence and extortion in a country where police have treated gender nonconformity as evidence of criminality.
tangentialFactors:
Dating apps carry a specific entrapment risk inside Nigeria. The Thomson Reuters Foundation reported in April 2024 on kito gangs that lure LGBTQ+ Nigerians through Grindr and comparable apps to meetings where victims are beaten, filmed and blackmailed with threats of outing.

Trans people in Nigeria have been killed with apparent official indifference. In August 2024 the beaten body of a 33-year-old transgender woman, a TikToker known as Abuja Area Mama, was found on an Abuja highway hours after she posted about visiting her boyfriend; the police described the deceased as a man fully dressed in female clothing. The Dial reported in February 2025 that six months after the killing no suspects had been charged.

Gender expression sits in active legislative contention. Reuters reported in September 2022 that transgender Nigerians live in fear of proposals to criminalise cross-dressing in public; whether those proposals have been enacted is not settled by the sources available here.

The imprisonment of Bobrisky (Idris Okuneye), the country's most prominent transgender woman, illustrates detention risk for a trans visitor. She pleaded guilty to four counts of naira abuse on 5 April 2024, was sentenced on 12 April 2024 to the maximum six months with no option of fine, and served it in a maximum-security prison in Lagos before release on 5 August 2024. Press coverage at sentencing openly debated which prison would hold the crossdresser, indicating that placement between male and female sections was left to discretion. An October 2024 investigative panel dismissed bribery allegations but found that housing her in a maximum-security prison violated the Nigerian Correctional Service Act because she was a first-time offender.

Extortion of men perceived as gay by police is routine. TimesLIVE reported in March 2025 that Okafor, a 24-year-old stopped by Lagos police, was struck in the mouth with a police gun butt and released only after paying almost half of the 50,000 naira bribe demanded, for looking gay.
localsOnly:
Residents of Rivers State live under the southern application of the Nigerian Criminal Code alongside the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act 2014, with no local protection statute and no statutory hate-crime provision covering sexual orientation or gender identity.

The 2022 judgment voiding Sections 4(1), 5(2) and 5(3) of the Same-Sex Marriage (Prohibition) Act is a nationwide ruling and therefore binds Rivers courts, removing those provisions as a basis for prosecuting LGBTQ+ organisations and individuals.

Human Rights Watch documented that arbitrary arrest and extortion by police became commonplace after the 2014 Act, with the case of eight of the 21 young men arrested and never charged at an Ibadan birthday party among the records of enforcement conduct.

Residents who report anti-LGBTQ+ violence to the police face the choice documented in the Port Harcourt case of Daniel, who was attacked and sexually abused in January 2015 and did not report the assault to the authorities.
outOfScopeNotes:
No Rivers State statute, enforcement pattern or court record specific to sexual orientation or gender identity appears in the sources reviewed; the jurisdiction's profile rests entirely on the national framework. Whether police in Port Harcourt apply the 2022 ruling limiting the 2014 Act, or continue to invoke the struck sections in practice, is unresolved here.

The status of the 2022 cross-dressing proposals reported by Reuters is unsettled by the available sources; whether any such prohibition has been enacted at national or Rivers level is not sourced.

No information was found on how a trans detainee would be classified or housed in a Rivers State correctional facility, and no Rivers-specific data on violence against trans people exists in these materials.
